Tumor metastasis leads to the vast majority of cancer related mortalities. Due to the inherent renegade status of a tumor, the spread of a cancer to new locations of the body is often unpreventable, leaving physicians with an intractable ailment and patients in the morgue. Tumor metastasis has classically been described as the movement of malignant tumor tissue from one organ to another, a process that normally takes place through the arterial transit system or through passages of lymph. Tumor cells detach from a primary tumor, travel and eventually invade other normal tissues. This is very dangerous, as new growth in an organ can quickly prevent its function. For example, a very small amount of metastatic tumor growth in a kidney can wipe out a great deal of nephron function, preventing proper fluid filtration.

Stephen Paget was a surgeon, and began noticing that secondary breast cancer tumors were often found in specific organs. He reported this in a journal in 1889, saying that the original tumor creates a "seed" that can only germinate in certain tissues, or "soils". This was not taken seriously and was forgotten until the famous parabiosis (parabiosis is literally sewing the arteries of two mice together) experiments of Hart and Fidler in the early 1980's. This was a big deal, and took awhile to catch on. Using radioactively labeled melanoma cells, Hart and Fidler were able to determine that “the outcome of metastasis is dependent on both tumor cell properties and host factors. This conclusion supports the "seed and soil" hypothesis to explain the nonrandom pattern of cancer metastasis” (Fidler and Hart, 1980).

You can read about Stephen Paget and his early discoveries on Wikipedia.
